nameStory: The Yellow Cellar Slug gets its name from two key traits: its yellowish coloration and its love of damp, dark places like cellars, basements, and crawl spaces. While many slugs prefer outdoor gardens, this species has adapted so well to human-made underground spaces that 'cellar' became part of its identity.
description: The Yellow Cellar Slug is a medium to large terrestrial slug that breathes air through a lung-like organ, making it quite different from water-dwelling mollusks. These slimy, soft-bodied creatures are gastropods - literally 'stomach-foot' - meaning they crawl along on their muscular belly. They're part of the keelback slug family, named for the ridge-like keel that runs along their back. As non-native residents of New England, they're most commonly found in human-created environments.

idTips.label: Body color and pattern
idTips.description: Yellowish to tawny brown body with darker spots or mottling, giving it a speckled appearance that feels slightly sticky to the touch

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Medium to large slug that can stretch several inches long when moving, with a robust, thick body that feels firm and muscular

idTips.label: Back ridge
idTips.description: Distinctive keel or ridge running along the back half of the body, visible as a raised line you can feel with gentle touch

idTips.label: Slime trail
idTips.description: Leaves a thick, persistent slime trail that feels quite sticky and takes time to dry, more substantial than smaller slug species

idTips.label: Tentacle behavior
idTips.description: Four tentacles that retract quickly when disturbed - two long ones with eyes at the tips and two shorter ones for smell and taste

habitat: Look for Yellow Cellar Slugs in damp, dark human-made spaces like basements, cellars, crawl spaces, and garages throughout New England. They also inhabit compost piles, under wooden boards, in greenhouses, and around building foundations where moisture collects. Unlike many native slugs, they're rarely found far from human habitation.

seasonality.spring: Active as temperatures warm and moisture increases, often found emerging from winter hiding spots in basements and foundations. Look for fresh slime trails on cellar walls.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid nights and rainy periods, retreating to cool, damp spaces during hot days. Peak feeding and movement occurs after summer thunderstorms.
seasonality.fall: Continues activity through mild autumn weather, often moving toward more protected winter sites like deeper in basements or under building foundations.
seasonality.winter: Becomes inactive in the coldest months but doesn't truly hibernate, occasionally spotted in heated basements or other consistently warm, damp spaces.

funFact: Yellow Cellar Slugs are hermaphrodites that perform an elaborate aerial mating dance - they hang from a shared strand of mucus while intertwined, sometimes spinning in circles high above the ground before exchanging sperm packets in mid-air!
confusionNotes: Often confused with other large garden slugs, but the Yellow Cellar Slug's preference for indoor spaces and its yellowish color with the distinctive back ridge help distinguish it. Remember: if you find a large yellowish slug in your basement, it's likely this species rather than outdoor garden varieties.
contextualKnowledge: This European native has become well-established in New England's human-modified environments, representing how some non-native species fill ecological niches created by human development. Unlike many invasive species, it rarely competes directly with native slugs since it prefers artificial habitats.
compareHints: As the only Limacus species commonly found in New England, compare it to other large slugs in the broader keelback family by noting its indoor habitat preference and yellowish coloration. Most other large slugs in the region prefer outdoor garden settings and tend to be darker gray or brown colors.
